title: Sacrifice to the Guru
hook: satgur vittahu vaariaa: a sacrifice to the Guru, meeting whom I remember the Master (Asa di Var, ang 470)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silk-cotton tree, and your line: useful, not tall. Who got your fruit? It's a week's end, too: ego and its cure, cartloads of books, the false king, the true heart, pain the medicine, sweetness, the tree. Today, the pauri that gathers them. Day five hundred fifty-three.
screen: `USEFUL, NOT TALL.` · `A WEEK: EGO, BOOKS, KOORH, TRUTH, SWEETNESS.`

segments.voice: A single sentence that rearranged everything. A book picked up by accident. A stranger on a train. Some lives turn on one afternoon like that. Ask what changed, though, and the answer is rarely the world. The street was the same street, the job the same job. What changed was the seeing. Back on day five hundred thirty-eight, Guru Nanak said he'd give himself a hundred times a day to the Guru who made angels out of men. Today's pauri comes back to that gratitude, and says exactly what changed.
screen: `A SENTENCE, A BOOK, A STRANGER.` → `THE SAME STREET, THE SAME JOB.` → `WHAT CHANGED WAS THE SEEING.`

segments.voice: The pauri is on ang 470, the same page as the tree and the scale. It opens: satgur vittahu vaariaa. I am a sacrifice to the True Guru. Vaariaa is a word of love and offering, the feeling behind the custom of circling something precious around a loved one's head and giving it away. Then, in paraphrase: meeting the Guru, I remembered the Master. The Guru gave the ointment of wisdom, and with these same eyes I now see the world as it is. Gian anjan. Anjan is the dark ointment people put along the eyes. The eyes don't change. What they can see does. That's the turning point. Before, the world was koorh, the false king and the tall tree, all looking solid and impressive. After, the same world is seen clearly, with the One in it. Then the pauri warns about the other road. Traders who leave the Master and attach to another, it says, are drowned. And it ends with a picture: the True Guru is the boat, though few realize it, and by grace the Guru carries people across. In Sikh teaching, the Guru is the One's word reaching a person: through the human Gurus, and now through the Guru Granth Sahib. In this pauri, the sacrifice is gratitude: offering yourself to whatever opened your eyes, and keeping them open. This week's saloks were all about seeing: ego, books, koorh, truth, pain, sweetness, the tree. Here's what lets you see them.
screen: `VAARIAA: I OFFER MYSELF.` · `GIAN ANJAN: WISDOM ON THE EYES.` · `THE SAME EYES, A NEW WORLD.` · `THE GURU IS THE BOAT.` · then, large: `THE TURNING POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a turning point. Sit and breathe out slowly. Let one moment come back when your way of seeing changed: a person, a line, a day. Picture the before and the after. Notice what you see now that you couldn't see then. If gratitude comes, let it come, toward the person, the moment, or, if you pray, toward the One behind them. If you'd like, you can say Waheguru, softly, as a thank-you. The bell holds the time.
Sacrifice to the Guru. Satgur vittahu vaariaa: I offer myself to the True Guru, who put wisdom on my eyes, so I see the same world truly.
Your line: the turning point. Today, look at one familiar thing, your street, your kitchen, a face, as if the ointment were fresh on your eyes, and see what's there. Day five hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this pauri in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and express gratitude to the Guru daily in Ardas and in bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: you've met the Guru and your eyes have been opened. what does the pauri say you now see?
options: a different world, far from this one.
this same world, seen as it really is.
nothing; the eyes close in meditation.
fork.reveal: the Guru gave the ointment of wisdom, and with these eyes the world is seen. the eyes don't change; what they see does.

original.note: Gurmukhi: I am a sacrifice to the True Guru; the opening of the pauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: sacrifice means giving something up.
what it means: offering yourself in gratitude to the Guru who opened your eyes to the same world, seen truly.
what a scholar hears: vaarna is the gesture of circling something around a loved one and giving it away; the pauri pairs it with gian anjan, wisdom's eye-salve.

notes: Pauri number given as 13; confirm. Paraphrase: sacrifice to the True Guru, meeting whom the Master is remembered; ointment of wisdom (gian anjan) so with these eyes the world is seen; traders who leave the Master and attach to another are drowned; the True Guru is the boat, few realize, by grace carries across.
The custom of vaarna (circling money or an offering around a loved one's head and giving it away) is offered as the feeling behind vaariaa; confirm.
Callback to day 538 (balihaaree gur aapne, Ang 462) is by another writer's day; confirm ang.

Fresh review: hook ('Most people can point to one', telling the listener what they feel) and carry (send a thank-you) repeated day 538's teacher-and-thanks angle; hook now leads into seeing, and the carry uses the eye-ointment image. 'Ten Gurus' count cut; the claim about what sacrifice to the Guru never means narrowed to this pauri, since Sikh history also honors martyrdom.
